facts.fact: T. R. Roberts described the species in 1989 in Memoirs of the California Academy of Sciences No. 14.
Its type locality is Tapah Fisheries Station in Perak, Malaysia, and the holotype is CAS-SU 39403.
It is a spiny eel of the family Mastacembelidae. Spiny eels are not true eels.
The name notophthalmus refers to the dark bar that extends below the eye.
The genus name Mastacembelus comes from Greek words meaning 'bite' and 'to throw oneself'.
It has a dark vertical bar below the eye, which M. unicolor, M. erythrotaenia and M. favus lack.
The back is mostly dark brown with irregular yellowish vermiculated marks. The belly is yellowish, with a faint, incomplete dark brown horizontal stripe.
The dorsal, anal and caudal fins are yellowish with vertical dark brown bars.
Roberts gave 37–39 dorsal spines, 73–86 dorsal-fin rays, 69–85 anal-fin rays, 24–26 pectoral-fin rays and 15–18 caudal-fin rays.
It has more dorsal spines than related Indonesian species: 37, against 33–35 in M. unicolor, M. erythrotaenia and M. favus.
The snout ends in a small, flexible appendage that the fish uses to investigate its surroundings.
A row of separate dorsal spines stands in front of the soft dorsal fin.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern, assessed on 9 August 2019.
No active conservation measures exist, because data on its distribution, threats and population dynamics are lacking.
It is known from western Peninsular Malaysia, northern and central Sumatra, western Borneo, and the islands of Bangka and Belitung in Indonesia.

The video says the first Indonesian record was published in 2023 and was based on a single fish. The 2023 Belitung paper lists earlier records from Sumatra and Borneo, and the Bangka record came before Belitung.
In 2023 a single male was caught in a fish trap on Belitung Island, the southernmost record for the species.
A study recorded it on Bangka Island, Indonesia, which was then the southernmost record.
Its known range is probably underestimated, because few specimens turn up in general fish surveys.
It usually lives in large rivers with clear or slightly turbid water over a pebble or gravel bottom.
The Belitung fish came from a slow-flowing swamp with abundant water plants on the middle course of the Lenggang River.
It is a demersal, tropical freshwater fish.
It lives near the bottom and probes the substrate, cracks and crevices for food.
It is rarely seen in the hobby. A US shop, The Wet Spot Tropical Fish, supplied the video footage of it.
Local fishers eat it, so overexploitation is the main threat. Indonesia also has an active Mastacembelus fishery.
It is rarely met in fish surveys, and its population is poorly understood.
It needs a large bottom area rather than a tall tank.
It needs a tight-fitting lid, because spiny eels escape through small gaps.
No source gives water parameters for this species. Provide sand, wood, rocks and caves to retreat into.
It is a predator that finds small prey in the substrate by smell and with its sensitive snout: worms, aquatic insects and small crustaceans.
In the aquarium, offer frozen bloodworms, mysis, chopped earthworms and other meaty foods.
Newly imported fish may not recognise prepared foods as food at first.
FishBase estimates its trophic level at 3.9.
It is secretive, searches slowly and methodically, and can bury itself completely in sand.
It is harmless to humans.
There is no reliable information on its reproduction, either in the wild or in captivity.
